# Overview {.unnumbered}

*Last update: 16.10.2026*

These notes are for developers who want to add a model to bmm. They explain how the package is put together and walk through the steps of contributing a model, from setting up your system to opening the pull request.

bmm covers five kinds of tasks: continuous reproduction (mixture models, IMM, SDM), categorical recall and n-AFC decisions (M3), processing-tree models (MPT), detection, recognition and confidence judgments (the signal detection models), and choices with response times (DDM, EZDM, Censored-Shifted Wald). `bmm_models()` lists them. The package requires **R \>= 4.1.0** and uses the native pipe `|>` throughout.

This guide describes bmm at the **v1.4.1** tag. Anything merged after that tag may not be reflected here yet. If you run into problems, [open an issue on GitHub](https://github.com/popov-lab/bmm/issues).

## How to read these notes {.unnumbered}

1.  [System setup](setup.qmd) and [Git workflow](git-workflow.qmd) get you a working fork.
2.  [Code structure](bmm-architecture.qmd) explains what happens when a user calls `bmm()`, and [Example models](example-model.qmd) shows two real model files.
3.  [Adding a new model](add-new-model.qmd) is the step-by-step guide, ending with a checklist for the pull request.
4.  [Coding conventions](coding-conventions.qmd) lists what review will check your code against.

The appendix, [Reference](reference.qmd), collects details you need only when you hit a particular problem, such as within-chain threading or a parameter name that collides with brms.

## The rules for contributing {.unnumbered}

Which branch to target, what a pull request must contain, how many reviews it needs and how model fits for articles are handled are set out in bmm's [CONTRIBUTING.md](https://github.com/popov-lab/bmm/blob/develop/.github/CONTRIBUTING.md). These notes do not repeat those rules. For a new model, two things matter from the start:

-   **Open an issue with the `new_model` template first**, so that you agree with the maintainers that the model fits the package and in which release it will appear.
-   **Make the model easy to check.** The reviewer reads your likelihood against its published source and looks at your parameter recovery. Include a short, runnable example with a small simulated dataset, and say in the pull request how long it takes to fit and what output to expect.
